title: Glove Rubber
passages:
The tender's engine idled quiet at the ore stub, steam curling off its heat exchangers into air cold enough to crack pipe. Coombs leaned against the cab rail, slate dark in his palm, and watched Rhea approach with the bound woman between her and Kass.

"Short hold," Rhea said. "Ore line's iced past the trestle. Your board won't clear a crew it can't name, and you know it."

Coombs tilted his head. "Board clears what I tell it. But the ice — " He glanced up the dark siding where the rails vanished into fog. " — that's a wait either way. How long?"

"Until the board gets a name it believes. Hour, maybe two." Rhea didn't blink. "Ivo's on mains power in the shop. Compressor priority just came back. We move her inside, reader two gives you a name, you get your clearance. Everybody eats."

"Everybody," Coombs repeated. "Including the lid-hand with the bay number for a name."

"Including her." Rhea jerked her chin at the relay shop door. "Teodoro's watching the board. He'll vouch for the hold."

Coombs laughed, low and rough. "Teodoro vouches for breathing. You want me to park a coast tender on Anza's ore stub for an hour on *maybe*? My schedule — "

"Your schedule's already broken," Kass said from behind Wren's shoulder. "Four rigs vanished off Kettering's master board. One had badge 2241 locked on channel when it went dark. Your slate didn't catch that, did it?"

Coombs's smile thinned. "Slate reads bodies. Not ghosts."

"Then read this one." Kass shoved Wren forward a half-step. "She rode the tool void from Kettering. Counted the seals aloud at Bay four. The forger stamped, she held the lid. You want the name behind the bay number? Take it inside."

The shop smelled of ozone, hot oil, and the sharp sweet of compressor coolant. Ivo sat propped against the workbench, respirator hose snaking from the mains feed into the patched diaphragm at his throat. The patch — a coin of heavy rubber, edges feathered into the seal — moved with each breath. Teodoro sat at the board desk, readers dark, one hand on the comms key.

"She comes in, reader two goes live," Teodoro said without turning. "Reader two reads *people*, not cargo. Whatever it names goes onto the living plate. Morning desk at Kettering reads that plate. You understand what that means for her."

"She understands," Rhea said. "Don't you."

Wren's taped wrists flexed at her sides. The seal tape creaked. She didn't look at Ivo, or the board, or the reader mount above the bench. Her eyes stayed on the gray work glove Kass set down on the steel — tape across one knuckle, a clean disc punched from the palm like a coin from a die.

"Found it in the tool void," Kass said. "Miko confirmed. Second person rode the void down the ore line. Counting numbers in the dark."

Teodoro finally turned. His gaze moved from the glove to Wren's bound hands, then to Rhea. "Reader two's hot. You want the match, you put the hands under it. But once it sings — "

"It sings," Rhea said. "That's the point."

She stepped to the reader mount, wiped frost from the sensor glass, and keyed the override. The board chimed, a single clean tone. The living-crew plate at reader two flickered, waiting.

"Knuckles first," Teodoro said. "Then the glove. Order matters."

Rhea looked at Wren. "Your turn."

Wren put her bound hands flat on the reader glass like she was returning something she'd already lost.

"Knuckles down," Teodoro said. "Don't help it."

Reader two was a dinner-tray of sensor glass on a jointed stalk, and it read hands the way Coombs's slate read walks: knuckle, tendon, the set of a thumb, the callus ridge where a person grips. It had no name field. That was the whole problem with it. Give it a hand, it gives you back a job.

The wrist loop had to come up half an inch to get her knuckles square on the glass. Rhea peeled the corner back with two fingers. The seal tape's printed strip logged the lift with a small dry click, and Coombs made a note on his slate without being asked.

"That's a break on my log," he said.

"Log it as weather," Kass said.

The frost under Wren's hands went clear in a widening ring. The plate took its time, three passes, the third slow enough that Ivo's respirator cycled twice in the quiet — the patched diaphragm at his throat folding and unfolding, a coin of heavy rubber moving like a slow eyelid. Wren looked at the wall behind the bench.

Then the plate chimed and printed to the board in plain type: BAY FOUR. SHIFT TWO. LID-HAND. The name slot sat empty above it, a blank line where a person goes.

"There's your clearance," Rhea said to Coombs.

"That's a job with a bay number," Coombs said. "I've hauled worse."

Kass set the gray glove under the glass, palm up, the punched hole pointed at the sensor. Tape across one knuckle. The reader went over it twice.

"Object," it said. "Work glove, left, heavy. Palm: disc absent. Edge die-cut, clean. Flag: missing part."

"Missing part," Teodoro repeated. "It flags a hole the way it flags a finger."

"Then it's the same hole," Kass said.

The plate compared. The two sets of knuckles agreed — the glove's taped knuckle and the woman's taped wrist, the same grip, the same hand — and it collapsed them into one entry, one body, one line on the living plate: LID-HAND, BAY FOUR, SHIFT TWO. Underneath, it pulled the archive and laid the old record beside the new one like two photographs of the same door. SEAL 21:47. BOX FOUR. HANDS PRESENT, TWO. HANDS LOGGED, ONE.

"Two present, one logged," Teodoro said. "That's not my line. That's the desk's line."

"Then wipe it," Rhea said.

"Can't. Reader two doesn't wipe. It only writes." He tapped the plate glass with a fingernail. "That's what I told you outside. Whatever it names, Kettering reads."

The comms key lit amber.

Teodoro looked at it for a second longer than a man who tells you everything he knows should need. "Morning desk. They watched the plate take a live entry and they want to know which Anza reader wrote it."

"Tell them reader two's down for service," Rhea said.

"They can see it's not." He put two fingers on the key and didn't press. "They'll ask again in ten minutes. Then they'll send somebody who doesn't ask."

Wren's hands were still on the glass, the peeled tape lifting at the corner, the hole in the glove beside them catching the shop light. She said, to nobody, "It's a hole. Holes don't get names."

"Yours did," Kass said.

Rhea looked at the number the reader had printed — *disc absent, die-cut, clean* — and then, for half a second, at her brother's throat, where the patch folded and unfolded and folded again.

Rhea crossed the shop in three steps and picked the glove up off the steel. She didn't put it back under the glass. She turned the palm to the work light and pushed her thumb into the hole, and the hole took her thumb to the first knuckle and stopped.

"Forty-one," she said.

"Forty-one what," said Kass.

"Millimeters." Rhea pulled the slide gauge out of her chest pocket — a steel rule with a jaw that slides and reads a gap to the hundredth — and set the jaws across the punch hole. "Forty-one oh-two."

Ivo's respirator cycled. The coin at his throat folded, unfolded. "She's got a hole in her glove the size of my windpipe," he said, and it came out in pieces, and he looked pleased with himself for spending the air.

Rhea went down on one knee at her tool roll, which lay open under the bench where she'd dropped it two days ago and not touched since. She came up with the gasket punch: a hollow steel tube on a T-handle, the thing you twist through rubber to bite a disc out clean. She held it beside the hole.

"There's a chip out of the rim," she said. "Four o'clock. Been there since Kettering, I don't know how." She turned the glove so the lamp caught the edge of the punch hole. "Same bite. Same place. Same depth."

"Say the plain version," Coombs said from the doorway. He had his slate up but he wasn't writing on it.

"The plain version is I cut my brother's diaphragm out of this glove." Rhea stood. "Past the second relay, in the dark, with him going grey in the cab. The membrane — the flexible part that actually pushes the air — had a tear in it the length of my thumbnail. I had no stock. I had a work glove in the rig's void. So I bit a disc out of the palm with this punch, feathered the edge into the seal, and I threw the rest of the glove back in the void because I had other problems."

Teodoro had gone very still at the board desk. "That's the same glove."

"That's the same glove," Rhea said. "Reader two doesn't lie about holes. It said die-cut, clean. My punch is the only die in this shop."

"So." Coombs lowered the slate an inch. "In my line we call that a mitigating circumstance."

"Your line has a field for it?"

"My line has a bunk for it." He shrugged, genial as a stove. "Desk won't. Desk has eleven seals short and a red file with Anza's name on it."

"Then the desk can read a caliper." Rhea set the glove down flat, hole up, and turned around. "You. Lid-hand. Bay four, shift two. Somebody cut a disc out of your palm and it's been in my brother's throat for two days, and I want to know how."

Wren's eyes came off the wall behind the bench for the first time. She looked at the glove, then at Ivo, then at the floor between her boots.

"You want it in writing," she said.

"I want it in sequence." Rhea's voice didn't rise. That was the thing about her; when it mattered she got quieter and more exact. "The med rig came into my node with its transponder pulled and its databus cut, and I found that glove in the void because I was elbow-deep in there hunting a fuse. A rig that doesn't post to any board, doesn't answer a hail, and doesn't exist. Now you tell me you rode that same void from Kettering to Anza with your hands taped and numbers in your mouth." She pointed at the hole. "So. How does a lid-hand's glove get into a dead rig's void, and why is there a hole in the palm the exact size of the patch keeping my brother upright?"

Nobody said anything. Ivo breathed. The tape on Wren's wrists creaked as she flexed them, once.

Coombs wrote something on his slate anyway.

Then the comms key stopped being amber. It went to a steady white, which on Teodoro's board didn't mean a queue — it meant a warm channel with somebody's actual hand on the other end of it.

Teodoro looked at it. "That's not a request," he said. "That's a person."

Wren answered the glove first, because it was the smaller question.

"I took it off to run the tape," she said. "You can't pull seal tape tight with a glove on. You lose the feel." She turned her bound wrists up so the printed strip caught the light. "Did the wrists with my teeth and the one hand. The glove went behind the fuse tray in the void, because I wanted the hand back."

Rhea's jaw set. "My hand was in that tray inside the hour. Hunting a fuse."

"Then we shook hands in the dark," Wren said, "and neither of us noticed."

Ivo laughed, which cost him three breaths and the use of his face for a second. Nobody else did.

"Ask the rest," Wren said.

"Fine." Rhea folded her arms. "Sequence."

"Seals are numbered," Wren said. "Every seal on a box carries a number, and the book has to agree with the box, so somebody stands at the lid and calls the numbers out loud as they go on. That's the lid-hand's whole job. You hold the lid square so the edge seats flat, and you call, and if the book and the box don't match, the rig doesn't load and nobody eats."

"And at 21:47."

"At 21:47 the box was already down and I was on the last seal. Bay four dash nine. I called it, and then I looked in the gap at the end of the lid, the way you do, to watch the seal seat." She said it evenly, like reading a gauge. "There was a man under it. Face up. Eyes open. Not making noise."

Kass didn't move. "And?"

"So I gave him the count the box gets." Wren's taped wrists creaked. "Three. Two." She stopped. "The stamp came down and I stopped at two and I never said one. The forger said log it, and I logged it."

"There's a reading," Wren said, before anyone asked. "You want the reading."

"Give it," Coombs said.

"Pod repeater held thirty-six point four. Last good, they call it — the last number the box got away with before its databus went quiet. Cold box, warm number. I read it off the slate at the stub and wrote it in the book against the seal, and that's the end of him." She looked at the steel bench, not at anybody. "He went cold at thirty-six four. I'm the hand that held the lid. Write that in the name slot if you're going to write anything."

Coombs turned his slate face-out so she could see her own line on it: WALK MATCH. VOICE MATCH. NO ROSTER.

"I don't need the count," he said. "Counts are for desks. I came for a body that walks off a roster and I've got one." He thumbed the glass dark and slid it into his coat. "In twenty-two years of pulling, the ones I catch lie to me about the weather. You gave me the truth before I asked for it. That's rare enough that I'd like to know what you think it buys you."

"Nothing," Wren said. "It's just what's in the book."

"Then it's the only honest line I've read all week."

"You didn't stamp," Kass said to her.

"Stamping's paper." Wren's voice didn't change at all. "I'm the hands."

Teodoro turned his board glass so the archive sat facing the room. "Reader two pulled it up beside you when it matched the knuckles. Seal 21:47, box four, hands present two, hands logged one. It doesn't wipe. It only writes." He tapped the empty line above LID-HAND. "And that slot has been blinking since it wrote you."

Rhea didn't argue with any of it. She set the gray glove down flat, hole up, and looked at her brother's throat, where the coin of heavy rubber folded and unfolded and folded again, keeping him in the room.

The comms key stopped being white.

Teodoro keyed it, and the shop filled with a woman's voice, unhurried, the voice of somebody reading off a screen in a warm room two hundred miles north. "Anza relay, Kettering morning desk. We're reading a live lid-hand on your plate. Bay four, shift two, name slot empty. Confirm you're holding her."

Teodoro looked at Wren. Wren looked at the floor between her boots.

"Anza," the voice said. "Your chain went green at oh eight hundred. Keep it that way."

The channel clicked shut, and the plate's empty slot kept blinking.

Coombs tapped his coat where the slate rode. "Tender rolls at the bell," he said. "That part hasn't moved."

Rhea didn't take the count. She didn't take Wren's word, either — that was the whole trouble with her, and everyone in the shop knew it. A mouth could say *thirty-six four* until it went dry and it wouldn't move her a millimeter. A readout would.

"Where's the living plate," she said.

"Right of the archive." Teodoro tipped his head at the reader stalk. "That's the one Kettering reads. Reader two writes a body to it, the body's crew till somebody countersigns it off. That's the rule. Living means living on the plate."

Rhea wiped the frost off the second pane of glass with her sleeve. The living-crew plate was smaller than the archive, a hand's width of lit glass, and it took a breath to resolve out of the cold. She read it the way she read a torque spec, top line down, no skipping.

She got to the fourth entry and stopped.

"Say it out loud," Kass said.

"Marlowe." Rhea's finger didn't leave the glass. "Living crew. Entered off the pod at Kettering, discharged twenty-one forty-seven." She moved down a line. "Countersigned. Live seal. Ospina, Bay four, seal authority." Another line. "Aboard two days. Shop-hand duty, this node." She looked up. "No hedge. No *presumed*, no *pending*, no asterisk. Living means living on the plate, you said."

"That's what I said."

"Then read your own machine." Rhea stepped back from the reader so the lit glass faced the room. "Twenty-one forty-seven. That's your seal. That's your box. And your box got up two days ago and it's on Anza's plate as crew with a real seal under it."

The shop went quiet enough that Ivo's respirator filled it — the coin at his throat folding, unfolding, folding. Wren's bound wrists had gone still.

"Thirty-six four," Wren said. It wasn't an argument. It was the number, back in her mouth where she'd kept it. "The repeater said thirty-six four."

"The repeater said last good." Rhea turned to her, and her voice dropped the way it did when it counted. "You said it yourself. Cold box, warm number. A number that got away before the box went quiet. You read a frozen number off a dead line and wrote it against a live man and called that the end of him." She tapped the plate glass, once, the way Teodoro had. "Machines don't lie about holes and they don't lie about crew. That's why I read them and not you."

Wren stared at the fourth line like it was written in a language she'd sealed shut.

"That's not — " she started.

"That's the plate," Rhea said. "You want to argue with it, take it up with the glass."

Coombs had his slate half out of his coat, and for once he wasn't writing on it. He looked at the living plate, then at the woman with the bay number for a name, and something moved behind the genial set of his face that didn't have a field on his log.

"Hands present, two," he said slowly. "Hands logged, one. That's the line the desk flagged." He thumbed the slate dark without reading it. "You've been carrying a dead man in your mouth for two days, and he's been in the next room breathing on a shop compressor the whole time."

"Don't," Wren said.

"I'm not saying anything." Coombs put the slate away. "Bell's still the bell."

Rhea was already looking at the door to the back room, the one behind the cathode with the light bleeding under it, where a man she'd never met was entered on her node's plate as alive.
